title: Shouldn't We Just Have Students Teach Themselves?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Using his own experience teaching himself piano chords via YouTube against his family's formal piano lessons, Stuart interrogates the popular narrative that self-directed learning outperforms traditional instruction. He warns against basing school-design decisions on anecdote, rhyming slogans ("drills kill"), or single studies, arguing instead for reasoning from first principles. His key move is naming what's invisible in "look how easy self-teaching is" stories: extensive prior knowledge and experience — in his case, years of self-taught guitar — that made his piano self-teaching possible and low-risk. Running his own experience through his five-key-beliefs framework (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy), he shows that his adult-level prior knowledge, not the self-directed method itself, is what generated his motivation. He concludes children, lacking this depth of prior experience and metacognitive maturity, still need expert-guided instruction — not because self-direction is worthless, but because motivation for self-teaching is downstream of prior knowledge children haven't yet built.
points: Stuart's central caution: school-design conclusions shouldn't be drawn from anecdote, rhyming slogans ("drills kill"), buzzy TED talks, or even single studies — decisions should be reasoned from first principles.

His key insight is that self-teaching success stories hide the role of prior knowledge — in his case, years of self-taught guitar experience made his piano self-teaching a low-risk, high-confidence undertaking.

He runs his own experience through the five key beliefs (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy) to show his self-directed motivation was downstream of adult-level prior knowledge, not the self-teaching method itself.

His conclusion is that children need expert-guided instruction not because they're lesser, but because they lack the depth of prior knowledge and metacognitive maturity that made his own adult self-teaching viable.
quotes: First of all, we should never base decisions about school on anecdotal evidence ("I hated piano drills growing up"), rhyming slogans ("drills kill"), or buzzy TED talks. Heck, we shouldn't even base them off the findings of single studies.

Second, what's invisible in my story (and in most "Holy cow learning new stuff is easier than we make it out to be in schools!" stories) is the role that my prior knowledge plays in both my motivation and in my success.

This has allowed me to play hundreds of hours of bedtime guitar for my children over the years, and these hundreds of hours have proven to me, beyond doubt, that there's a way to "learn enough" on the guitar to have it increase one's quality of life.

My prior knowledge completely predicts my level of motivation for learning the piano. It also ensures that I'll approach practicing piano intelligently, with full engagement in the design of my practice.
A child, on the other hand, is at the start of the lifelong learning journey. She needs to be shown, by an expert, how to learn piano.
So no: students shouldn't teach themselves. We can love and honor and respect and value our children without blindly assuming that their ability to teach themselves is the same as that of an adult.
